mentions.quote: Bhṛgu says one should ascertain the truth by means of a divine ordeal, even when good witnesses are present.
Bhṛgu has declared these to be classes.
Bhṛgu says it is of a different time.
Bhṛgu says it is not a capital case there.

entities.description: Ancient sage and legal authority cited multiple times as a source for procedural rules on ordeals and witness classes.
entities.justification: Bhṛgu is explicitly named as an authoritative source across chapters 24, 29, 30, and 32, establishing evidentiary and ordeal rules.

mentions.quote: that statement of the witness is admissible; otherwise, it is not, says Bṛhaspati.

entities.description: Sage and legal authority cited for the rule that witness testimony is only admissible when the witness was present before both parties.
entities.justification: Bṛhaspati is named as the source of an admissibility rule for witness statements in chapter 29.

mentions.quote: Manu says one should not abandon an accused person.

entities.description: Foundational lawgiver cited as authority for the rule that accused persons must not be abandoned in dispute proceedings.
entities.justification: Manu is explicitly cited in chapter 33 as the source of a normative rule about the treatment of accused persons.

mentions.quote: the king should accept the human proof in that case, not the divine ordeal.
The king himself should examine the witnesses who are present.
he should determine the defects of the document after deliberating with Brahmins.
A king should reject divine ordeals even if given according to the rules, if they were administered by the foolish, greedy, or wicked.
A king, judging thus, is not deprived of righteousness and wealth.

entities.description: The king is the supreme judicial officer who oversees trials, examines witnesses, evaluates documents, and administers ordeals in civil and criminal disputes.
entities.justification: The king appears throughout chapters 24–36 as the central figure of the judicial process, with explicit duties to examine witnesses, accept proof, and supervise ordeals.

mentions.quote: The Chief Judge, in the presence of the plaintiff and defendant, should appoint all the witnesses in the courtroom.
The scribe, the Chief Judge, and the assessors in order, when a case is being decided in the king's sight, are declared to be witnesses.
the village, the Chief Judge, and the king, for the litigants.

entities.description: The Chief Judge presides over the courtroom in the king's presence, appoints and questions witnesses, and may himself serve as a witness.
entities.justification: The Chief Judge is named as a distinct judicial officer in chapters 29 with specific procedural duties.

mentions.quote: after the victory has been determined by the assessors.
the decision of the assessors, the Chief Judge, or the family councils should be entered.
Hidden defects are to be revealed by the assessors at the proper time by showing the scriptures.
The scribe, the Chief Judge, and the assessors in order, when a case is being decided in the king's sight, are declared to be witnesses.

entities.description: Panel of learned men who evaluate evidence, determine victory in legal disputes, and may serve as witnesses when cases are decided in the king's presence.
entities.justification: Assessors are a recurring institutional group across chapters 24–29 with defined functions in evaluating proof and recording decisions.

mentions.quote: he should question the twice-born for true testimony, having them face north or east, in the forenoon, being himself pure and they being pure.
he should determine the defects of the document after deliberating with Brahmins.
to a Brahmin, the ordeal of the balance; avoiding poison for the best of the twice-born (Brahmin).
the wealth of a minor or a learned Brahmin, which comes from the mother's or father's side respectively.
those who have killed their mother, father, a Brahmin, a preceptor, a child, a woman, or a king

entities.description: The priestly varna, subject to the ordeal of the balance (not poison), whose property is protected, who serve as legal consultants and witness category.
entities.justification: Brahmins appear across chapters 24–33 in multiple roles: as consultants to the king, as witness groups, and as a specially protected caste category in ordeal law.

mentions.quote: To a Kshatriya, the ordeal of fire.

entities.description: The warrior/ruling varna, to whom the ordeal of fire is specifically assigned in legal disputes.
entities.justification: Kshatriyas are named in chapter 33 as the caste category specifically assigned the fire ordeal.

mentions.quote: to a Vaishya, one should apply the ordeal of water.

entities.description: The merchant/agricultural varna assigned the water ordeal in legal proceedings.
entities.justification: Vaishyas are named in chapter 33 in the caste-based ordeal assignment scheme.

mentions.quote: virtuous Shudras for Shudras, and those of the lowest castes for the lowest castes.
even if they are twice-born, one should treat them like Shudras (in ordeals).

entities.description: The servile varna whose members may only testify for fellow Shudras and whose ordeal treatment is used as a comparator for certain twice-born professionals.
entities.justification: Shudras appear in chapters 29 and 33 as a witness category and as the reference class for ordeal treatment of certain occupational groups.

mentions.quote: At the temple of Indra for those accused of major sins.

entities.description: The Vedic king of gods whose temple is prescribed as the site for ordeals in cases of major sins.
entities.justification: Indra's temple is named in chapter 34 as the sacred venue for serious ordeal proceedings.

mentions.quote: If there is testimony in a case of killing a living being, one should have it stated in the presence of Shiva.

entities.description: Hindu deity in whose presence testimony must be given in cases involving the killing of a living being.
entities.justification: Shiva is specified in chapter 30 as the divine presence before whom testimony on killing must be given.

mentions.quote: The opinion of the Smṛti scriptures should also be written therein.
those assessors present there who are learned in the Smṛti scriptures.

entities.description: The body of remembered law-texts whose opinions are to be recorded in judicial documents and which assessors must be learned in.
entities.justification: Smṛti scriptures are invoked in chapter 25 as a required element of judicial records and as the knowledge base for qualified assessors.

mentions.quote: one should have the testimony given through a document sent by three men learned in the Vedas.
For students of the Vedas, a period of twelve years is prescribed.
mentions.role: field of study governing possession rights

entities.description: The canonical Vedic scriptures whose study defines student status (protecting property rights) and whose scholars may transmit testimony by document.
entities.justification: The Vedas appear in chapters 27 and 29 as the standard of qualification for both proxy witness and student status with legal implications.

mentions.quote: For those born of mixed unions against the natural order, the divine ordeal should be given at a crossroads.

entities.description: A public intersection designated as the proper site for ordeals involving persons of mixed-caste birth.
entities.justification: The crossroads is named in chapter 34 as a specific ritual location for a defined category of ordeal subjects.

mentions.quote: To a Kshatriya, the ordeal of fire.
For a loss of eighty, one should indeed administer the ordeal of fire.
One should not apply the ordeal of fire to blacksmiths.
One should avoid the ordeal of fire for lepers.
If the accused stumbles or is burnt in a place other than the designated spot, the gods do not consider him burnt.

entities.description: A divine ordeal by fire assigned to Kshatriyas and calibrated to losses of eighty gold pieces, with procedural rules about valid burning and contraindications for certain persons.
entities.justification: The fire ordeal is substantively described across chapters 32–35 with rules for assignment, calibration, and procedure.

mentions.quote: to a Vaishya, one should apply the ordeal of water.
For a loss of sixty, the ordeal of water should be given.
When the arrow is shot, the submersion should be done, and the going (of the retriever) should be simultaneous.
If only the top of his head is visible, but not his ears or his nose, one should declare him pure.

entities.description: A divine ordeal by submersion in water, assigned to Vaishyas and calibrated to losses of sixty gold pieces, with detailed procedural rules for administering and reading the result.
entities.justification: The water ordeal is described across chapters 32, 33, and 36 with caste assignment, value calibration, and a detailed procedural account.

mentions.quote: for a loss of one hundred, the ordeal of poison is prescribed.
avoiding poison for the best of the twice-born (Brahmin).
one should never give poison to those who know mantras and yoga.

entities.description: The most severe divine ordeal, calibrated to the highest value losses (one hundred gold pieces) and prohibited for Brahmins and those who know mantras and yoga.
entities.justification: The poison ordeal is described in chapters 32 and 33 with its value threshold and its contraindications.

mentions.quote: to a Brahmin, the ordeal of the balance.
for forty, indeed the ordeal of the balance.
For those suspected by kings, one should employ the ordeal of the balance and others.
If the sling breaks, or the balance beam, or the cord, or if there is doubt about the purity, one should test the man again.

entities.description: A divine ordeal by weighing, assigned to Brahmins and calibrated to losses of forty gold pieces, with procedural rules for equipment failure.
entities.justification: The balance ordeal is described across chapters 32–34 with caste assignment, value calibration, and procedural details.

mentions.quote: For a loss of twenty or ten, the drinking of consecrated water is prescribed.
one should administer only the ordeal of consecrated water.
The ordeal of consecrated water should not be administered by the wise to drunkards, those addicted to women, and gamblers.

entities.description: A divine ordeal by drinking sacred water, prescribed for moderate losses (ten to twenty gold pieces) and for cases of suspicion, but forbidden for gamblers, drunkards, and atheists.
entities.justification: The consecrated water ordeal is described in chapters 32–33 with value calibration, prescribed uses, and specific prohibitions.

mentions.quote: whatever custom has been declared for guilds, corporations, assemblies, and the like, the proof for it is a document.
The established custom of learned Brahmins, cities, guilds, assemblies, and citizens.
Ascetics, members of guilds and corporations, and groups of merchants, and others who are in groups.

entities.description: Organized trade or professional bodies whose established customs are provable only by document, and whose members form a distinct witness class.
entities.justification: Guilds appear across chapters 24, 25, and 29 as legal entities whose customs require documentary proof and as a defined witness class.

themes.topic: Hierarchy of evidence: preference of human over divine proof

mentions.quote: When witnesses are available, a wise man should avoid a divine ordeal.
the king should accept the human proof in that case, not the divine ordeal.
If human proof is available, even if it covers only a part of the case, it should be accepted, and not a divine ordeal, even if it is complete.

themes.justification: Chapter 24 systematically establishes that human evidence (document, witnesses) is preferred over divine proof whenever available, constituting the foundational evidentiary principle of the text.

themes.topic: Caste as a structuring principle in legal procedure

mentions.quote: Women should give evidence for women, similar twice-born for the twice-born, virtuous Shudras for Shudras.
To a Kshatriya, the ordeal of fire; to a Brahmin, the ordeal of the balance; to a Vaishya, one should apply the ordeal of water.
Whatever kind of person is to be proven by the plaintiff, he should prove it with similar persons.

themes.justification: Across chapters 29 and 33, the text explicitly calibrates both witness eligibility and the type of divine ordeal to the caste of the litigants, revealing caste as a pervasive organising principle of dharmaśāstra procedure.

themes.topic: Procedural purity and ritual validity of ordeals

mentions.quote: Those (ordeals) given at an improper time or place, or performed outside, undoubtedly cause a miscarriage of justice in all matters.
A king should reject divine ordeals even if given according to the rules, if they were administered by the foolish, greedy, or wicked.
a divine ordeal should be administered by experts according to the prescribed procedure. One that is applied contrary to the rules is not capable of establishing the case.

themes.justification: Chapters 34–36 emphasise that ordeals derive their probative force from ritual correctness in time, place, and administrator — procedural invalidity nullifies the divine verdict.

themes.topic: The epistemic value of possession in property disputes

mentions.quote: A witness is superior to inference, a document is superior to witnesses, and possession, uninterrupted for three generations, is weightier than these.
just as milk, over time, produces curd endowed with flavor, so does possession, come down through three generations, become a cause for ownership over time.
If possession for three generations is independent, it is valid; if it is for a shorter period, it must be with title.

themes.justification: Chapter 27 develops the concept of multi-generational possession (tri-generational continuity) as surpassing even written documents, making it the apex of the evidentiary hierarchy for property.

themes.topic: Documentary integrity and the problem of forgery

mentions.quote: When letters are out of place, not in line, ambiguous, or lacking proper form, then the document becomes a forged document.
He who forges a document concerning immovable property, a sale, or a pledge, upon being duly convicted, should be made deprived of his tongue, hands, and feet.
Just as an image in a mirror, though unreal, appears real, so do skillful people create copies of documents.

themes.justification: Chapter 26 devotes substantial attention to the formal markers of forgery, the penalties for it, and the epistemological challenge of detecting false documents — framing forgery as the central threat to documentary evidence.

themes.topic: Temporal limitation and the lapse of legal rights

mentions.quote: A document that is past thirty years, and has not been seen or mentioned, does not attain validity, even if the witnesses are still present.
When an asset is enjoyed for twenty years by means of a document in the presence of a capable owner, that document is free from defect.
Uninterrupted by these three, possession for sixty years is considered firm.

themes.justification: Chapters 26–27 implicitly develop a statute-of-limitations doctrine through repeated time thresholds (20, 30, 60 years) that govern when documents become invalid and when possession becomes incontestable.

themes.topic: Moral character and ritual fitness as conditions of witness competence

mentions.quote: Those who are of renowned family and character, free from greed and delusion, trustworthy, pure, and distinguished—their testimony is beyond doubt.
Within a week, it becomes known where a witness speaks falsely: by disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman.
Those who live by the same profession, those who work for his service and benefit, his relatives, friends, and servants—they are his partisans and not witnesses.

themes.justification: Chapters 29–31 ground witness reliability in moral and ritual purity, and link false testimony to divine retribution — framing legal competence as inseparable from character.

themes.topic: Parity between parties as a principle of fair procedure

mentions.quote: One should never subject the plaintiff to a divine ordeal. A divine ordeal should be administered to the accused by those skilled in ordeals.
Whatever kind of person is to be proven by the plaintiff, he should prove it with similar persons. One should not ever prove a case with witnesses of a higher or lower station.
Where the witnesses are of equal standing, one should ascertain the truth there also by divine ordeals.

themes.justification: The text repeatedly insists that ordeals fall only on the accused (not the plaintiff) and that witnesses must match the social station of the parties, implicitly invoking a symmetry principle of equal treatment between litigants.

themes.topic: Exclusion of the morally corrupt from divine ordeals

mentions.quote: For those who have killed their mother, father, a Brahmin, a preceptor, a child, a woman, or a king; for those guilty of major sins.
The ordeal of consecrated water should not be administered by the wise to drunkards, those addicted to women, and gamblers, nor to those who live as atheists.
Especially for those guilty of major sins, for atheists, and for those who delight in the practice of sin, a divine ordeal should not be administered to them.

themes.justification: Chapter 33 establishes a substantial list of persons for whom divine ordeals are categorically forbidden, reflecting the theological premise that ordeals test the gods' verdict on persons presumed capable of truthful engagement.

themes.topic: Sign-reading and behavioral inference as evidentiary tools

mentions.quote: examination by means of reasoning, signs, gestures, appearance, speech, eyes, and actions of men.

Trembling, sweating, dejection, licking dry lips, drawing on the ground, shifting from one's place, looking sideways and upwards, and a change in voice—these the wise have declared to be the signs of a guilty person.
By his appearance, gestures, and movements, one should discern his state of mind. The defendant becomes defeated; he is marked by inference.

themes.justification: Chapters 24 and 30 describe a proto-forensic system of behavioral sign-reading as a supplement to formal proof, treating bodily and vocal signs as evidence of guilt.

citations.quote: Bhṛgu says one should ascertain the truth by means of a divine ordeal, even when good witnesses are present.
citations.justification: Bhṛgu is named as an authority who specifically overrides the general preference for witnesses in cases of the most serious violent crimes.

citations.quote: Bhṛgu has declared these to be classes.
citations.justification: Bhṛgu is cited as the authority for the classification of ascetics, guild members, and merchant groups as distinct witness classes.

citations.quote: Bhṛgu says it is of a different time.
citations.justification: Bhṛgu is cited for the rule that acts witnessed at different times must be testified to separately.

citations.cited_work: unspecified ruling on ordeals for suspected persons
citations.quote: Bhṛgu says it is not a capital case there.
citations.justification: Bhṛgu is cited to establish that ordeals for those tainted by public slander are not capital in nature.

citations.quote: that statement of the witness is admissible; otherwise, it is not, says Bṛhaspati.
citations.justification: Bṛhaspati is directly cited as the source for the rule that only eyewitness testimony from someone present before both parties is admissible.

citations.cited_work: unspecified ruling on the treatment of accused persons
citations.quote: Manu says one should not abandon an accused person.
citations.justification: Manu is directly cited as authority for the requirement that even morally problematic accused persons must not be abandoned in legal proceedings.
